Bandit based Monte-Carlo Planning

agz.lead: AlphaGo learned from thirty million human moves before it played itself. AlphaGo Zero starts from random weights and never sees a human game — and is stronger. The mechanism that makes that possible is treating tree search not as a way to play but as a way to generate training targets.

blocks.h: Search as a policy improvement operator
blocks.b:
This is the paper's central idea. Run MCTS from a position using the current network's policy as its prior; the visit counts that result are a **better** policy than the prior was, because search has looked ahead and corrected some of its mistakes.

So train the network's policy head towards the search's visit distribution, and its value head towards the game's eventual outcome:

$$\ell = (z - v)^2 - \boldsymbol{\pi}^{\top} \log \mathbf{p} + c\|\theta\|^2$$

where $\boldsymbol{\pi}$ is the normalised visit count and $z$ the result. The network chases the search; the improved network makes the next search better; that search produces better targets again. It is policy iteration with MCTS as the improvement step, and it needs no external data because the search generates its own supervision.

The loop bootstraps from random play, and the paper's learning curves show it passing the human-trained AlphaGo within days.

One network with two heads replaces the separate policy and value networks, sharing a residual convolutional trunk — the paper reports the combined network stronger than the two apart, since the two objectives regularise each other.

Rollouts are gone. Leaves are evaluated by the value head alone, where AlphaGo mixed it with a fast simulated playout. The hand-crafted features are gone: input is the raw board, plus a history of previous positions and the colour to play.

What remains is the board, the rules, and the loop. The reduction is the result — a much simpler system that is much stronger — and it is unusually clean evidence that the human data had been a scaffold rather than a foundation.

blocks.h: The exploration that keeps it moving
blocks.b:
A self-play loop can collapse: if the network becomes confident, search follows its prior, games become repetitive, and the training data stops containing anything new.

Two mechanisms prevent it. Dirichlet noise is added to the prior at the root of every search, so some unlikely moves are always tried. And early moves in self-play games are sampled from the visit distribution proportionally rather than greedily, so openings vary.

Both are small and both are load-bearing — a self-improvement loop with no source of novelty converges to a fixed point that may be far from optimal.

The requirements are strict and they are what confine the method. A **perfect simulator** is needed, since search plays out hypothetical positions — the rules must be known exactly and be cheap to apply. The game must be **deterministic** and fully observed. And the reward must be available at the end of a game with no ambiguity.

Go, chess and shogi satisfy all of this; almost nothing else does. AlphaZero generalises across those three by removing the remaining game-specific components, and MuZero attacks the simulator requirement itself by learning a latent dynamics model — which is the step that takes the family towards domains where the rules are not given.

refs.t: Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge
Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search

alphazero.lead: AlphaGo Zero removed the human data and remained a Go program, with Go-specific input planes and Go-specific augmentation. AlphaZero removes those too and runs the same algorithm, unchanged, on chess and shogi — beating the strongest specialised engine in each within hours.

blocks.b:
Three assumptions in AlphaGo Zero were Go's rather than the algorithm's.

**Symmetry.** Go's board is symmetric under eight rotations and reflections, which AlphaGo Zero exploits both to augment training data and to average evaluations during search. Chess is not symmetric — castling and pawn direction break it — so the augmentation is removed entirely.

**Binary outcomes.** Go cannot be drawn under the rules used; chess frequently is. The value head is retrained to estimate the expected outcome over win, draw and loss rather than a win probability.

**A fixed evaluation of self-play strength.** AlphaGo Zero maintained a best-so-far network and only replaced it after a challenger won a match by a margin. AlphaZero maintains one continuously updated network and does away with the evaluation matches, which is simpler and, the paper reports, no worse.

blocks.h: The contrast with the engines it beat
blocks.b:
Stockfish and Elmo are the product of decades of accumulated human chess and shogi knowledge — hand-tuned evaluation functions with hundreds of terms, opening books, endgame tablebases, and alpha-beta search with elaborate pruning heuristics.

AlphaZero has none of it. It knows the rules; everything else is learned from self-play. And its search is different in kind: alpha-beta examines tens of millions of positions per move, AlphaZero's MCTS examines tens of thousands, relying on the network to evaluate them far better rather than on volume.

The paper's analysis of its opening play — discovering and then discarding standard human openings, at rates it can measure — is the more interesting evidence, since it shows the system rediscovering and then re-evaluating a body of accumulated theory.

The claim being made is generality within a class, not generality outright. Chess, shogi and Go differ in board, pieces, move generation and outcome structure, and the same code and hyperparameters handle all three with only the rules module swapped.

That is a real result — the specialised-engine paradigm assumed the opposite — and it is bounded. The three games are all two-player, zero-sum, deterministic, perfectly observed, and equipped with an exact simulator.

Every one of those conditions is load-bearing. Search requires playing out hypothetical futures, which requires the rules; a stochastic environment breaks the tree; partial observation makes a position insufficient as a state.

So AlphaZero is at the end of a line that removed human knowledge and game-specific engineering, and cannot take the next step. MuZero does, by learning a latent dynamics model whose only requirement is that it predict reward, value and policy correctly — a model that need not resemble the environment at all, which is what lets the same method work on Atari where no rules are given.

refs.t: A general reinforcement learning algorithm that masters chess, shogi, and Go through self-play
Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge

muzero.lead: AlphaZero plans by playing out real moves in a real simulator, which confines it to domains whose rules are known. MuZero learns a model instead — but not a model of the environment. It learns a latent dynamics whose only obligation is to predict reward, value and policy correctly, which is all planning actually consumes.

blocks.b:
The usual instinct for model-based RL is to predict the next observation, and it fails in two ways: most of an observation is irrelevant detail, and reconstruction error is a poor proxy for planning usefulness. A model can render pixels beautifully and be useless for deciding what to do.

MuZero abandons reconstruction entirely. Three functions are learned jointly:

**Representation** $h$ maps the observation history to a latent state $s^0$. **Dynamics** $g$ maps $(s^{k}, a)$ to the next latent state and an immediate reward. **Prediction** $f$ maps a latent state to a policy and a value.

The latent has no prescribed meaning and is never decoded. It is trained only so that unrolling $g$ and reading $f$ reproduces the quantities search needs — the model is required to be *value equivalent* to the environment, not to resemble it.

For each trajectory the network is unrolled $K$ steps from a real observation, applying the real actions that were taken, and three losses are applied at every step: the predicted policy against the MCTS visit counts at that real timestep, the predicted value against an $n$-step bootstrapped return, and the predicted reward against the observed one.

Gradients flow back through the whole unroll into the dynamics and representation functions. Nothing supervises the latent state directly — it is shaped entirely by having to support those three predictions several steps ahead.

Search then runs entirely in latent space. MCTS expands nodes by applying $g$, with no environment interaction, so planning costs network evaluations rather than simulator calls.

MuZero matches AlphaZero on Go, chess and shogi without being given the rules, and simultaneously reaches state of the art on Atari — a domain the AlphaZero line could not touch, since Atari has no rules module, is stochastic in effect, and gives rewards throughout rather than at the end.

That one algorithm covers both is the result. Board games need deep, precise search; Atari needs perception and reactive control with shallow lookahead. The reward prediction in the dynamics function is what makes the second work, since intermediate rewards must be modelled rather than assumed absent.

blocks.h: The limits of a model that cannot be inspected
blocks.b:
The latent has no interpretation, so the model cannot be checked, debugged or reused for anything but the quantities it was trained to predict. Ask it a question outside that set — what does this state look like, is this transition physically possible — and there is no answer.

It is also trained on-distribution, so planning far from the visited data is unreliable in a way nothing detects: the model will confidently unroll into latent states that correspond to nothing.

And the compute is substantial. Search at every step during both training and acting, with a network evaluation per node, is expensive next to a model-free method — which is the standing trade of this whole track, bought in exchange for sample efficiency.

refs.t: Mastering Atari, Go, Chess and Shogi by Planning with a Learned Model
The Value Equivalence Principle for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

worldmodels.lead: An agent learning control from pixels must learn to see and to act from the same reward signal, which is a very thin channel for perception. World Models separates them into three components trained independently — a visual encoder, a dynamics model, and a tiny controller — and shows the controller can be trained entirely inside the learned model.

blocks.b:
**V** is a VAE that encodes a frame into a latent $z$ of a few tens of dimensions, trained by reconstruction on rollouts from a random policy. No reward is involved.

**M** is a recurrent network with a mixture-density output, predicting $p(z_{t+1} \mid z_t, a_t, h_t)$. Its output is a mixture of Gaussians with a temperature parameter, so uncertainty about the next observation is represented rather than averaged into a single prediction.

**C** is the controller, and it is deliberately tiny — a single linear layer mapping $[z_t, h_t]$ to an action, a few hundred parameters.

The asymmetry is the design. V and M hold nearly all the parameters and are trained by self-supervision on cheap data; C is the only part optimised against the task, and it is small enough for a derivative-free method — CMA-ES — to search directly, sidestepping the credit-assignment problem entirely.

Since M predicts the next latent given an action, it is a simulator. The paper trains the controller entirely on rollouts generated by M, never touching the environment, and then transfers the resulting policy back — it works.

The failure mode is what makes this interesting. A controller optimised against an imperfect model finds and exploits its inaccuracies, producing behaviour that scores brilliantly in the dream and fails in the world. The paper's mitigation is to raise the **temperature** of M's predictions, making the dream noisier so that its exploitable flaws are not reliable enough to depend on.

That is a blunt but honest answer to model exploitation, and it names the central difficulty of model-based RL: the optimiser is an adversary to the model's errors.

The reward signal in a control task is a scalar arriving occasionally. Using it to learn a convolutional encoder means the entire visual representation is supervised through that one channel, which is why model-free pixel-based agents need tens of millions of frames.

Reconstruction, by contrast, supervises every pixel of every frame. V learns a usable representation from random-policy data before any reward is seen, and M learns the dynamics from the same data. Only the last, tiny step needs the reward.

The cost is that V is trained on random-policy rollouts, so it encodes what a random agent sees. A good policy visits states the encoder was never fitted to, and nothing in the pipeline corrects that — the paper acknowledges the iterative version, alternating data collection and retraining, as necessary for harder tasks.

The paper is short, unusually readable, and its influence is out of proportion to its results. It made "learn a latent, plan in it" concrete at a time when model-based deep RL had little to show.

Dreamer is the direct successor, and its central change is to remove the separation: instead of training a small controller by evolution inside a frozen model, it backpropagates the policy gradient **through** the learned dynamics, so the model and the policy improve together. That is what turns the idea from a demonstration into a method competitive with the model-free state of the art.

refs.t: World Models
Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution

dreamer.lead: World Models trained a tiny controller by evolution inside a frozen dynamics model. Dreamer keeps the latent world model and makes it differentiable end to end — the policy gradient flows backwards through imagined rollouts into the actor — which turns the idea into a method competitive with the model-free state of the art.

blocks.b:
The world model carries a state with two parts: a deterministic recurrent component $h_t$ and a stochastic component $z_t$ sampled from a learned distribution. The split matters. A purely deterministic model cannot represent uncertainty about what happens next; a purely stochastic one struggles to remember information over long horizons, since noise is injected at every step.

Training maximises a variational bound with three reconstruction terms — observation, reward and episode continuation — plus a KL between the **posterior** state, which sees the current observation, and the **prior** state, which must predict it without. That KL term is the one that matters for planning: it is what forces the model to be able to imagine forward without seeing anything.

Once the dynamics are differentiable, the actor need not be trained by sampling returns. Dreamer rolls the model forward from encoded real states for a fixed horizon, evaluates the imagined trajectory with a learned critic, and differentiates that value **through the dynamics** with respect to the actor's parameters.

The gradient is analytic rather than an estimate — the same advantage the deterministic policy gradient has over REINFORCE, extended over a multi-step imagined rollout. The critic is trained on imagined trajectories too, with $\lambda$-returns balancing bias against variance.

Environment interaction is then only needed to keep the model honest, which is where the sample efficiency comes from: a few hundred thousand real steps for tasks that model-free methods need tens of millions for.

The first two versions worked well and needed per-domain tuning, which for a method claiming generality is the substantive objection. DreamerV3's contribution is mostly about scale invariance, so that one hyperparameter set works everywhere.

A **symlog** transformation, $\mathrm{sign}(x)\log(|x|+1)$, is applied to rewards and to reconstruction targets, so signals differing by orders of magnitude across domains are compressed into a comparable range. Values and rewards are predicted as **two-hot** distributions over a fixed set of bins rather than as scalars, which makes the regression robust to outliers. KL terms are clipped below a floor, so the model does not spend capacity driving an already-small divergence to zero.

With those, one configuration handles continuous control, Atari, and — the headline — collecting diamonds in Minecraft from scratch, a long-horizon sparse-reward task with no curriculum.

blocks.h: The model is still the ceiling
blocks.b:
Everything the actor learns comes from imagined rollouts, so a systematic model error becomes a systematic policy error, and the optimiser actively seeks out the model's mistakes — the exploitation problem World Models met and answered with noise.

Dreamer bounds it by keeping the imagination horizon short and by continually refitting the model on fresh data, which is mitigation rather than a solution. And the reconstruction objective spends capacity on visual detail regardless of whether it matters for control, which is exactly the criticism MuZero's value-equivalent model avoids by never reconstructing anything.

The two therefore represent the fork in model-based RL: reconstruct the world and plan in it, or learn only what planning consumes.

refs.t: Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination
Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models
Learning Latent Dynamics for Planning from Pixels

cql.lead: Offline reinforcement learning trains on a fixed dataset with no further interaction, and the standard algorithms fail badly at it — for a reason that is specific and diagnosable. The bootstrap queries $Q$ at actions the data never contains, those values are unconstrained, and the policy is trained to find whichever is highest.

blocks.h: Why the error is sought rather than averaged
blocks.b:
In online learning an overestimated action gets tried, produces a poor outcome, and is corrected. Offline that loop is broken: nothing tests the estimate, so an arbitrarily wrong value can persist and grow through the bootstrap.

The direction of the failure is what makes it fatal. The target $\max_{a'} Q(s', a')$ — or the actor maximising $Q$ — selects precisely the action whose value is most overestimated. Extrapolation error is not merely present but actively exploited, and the resulting policy is confidently wrong about actions no one has ever taken.

Empirically, off-policy algorithms trained on a fixed buffer often perform worse than behavioural cloning on the same data, which is a striking failure for methods that are nominally off-policy already.

blocks.h: Pushing down what the data does not support
blocks.b:
The prior approach was to constrain the policy to stay near the behaviour policy, which requires estimating that policy and is conservative in a way that ignores the value function entirely.

CQL instead regularises the **values**. A term is added to the critic's loss that pushes down $Q$ on actions sampled from the learned policy and pushes up on actions actually present in the data:

$$\min_{Q} \; \alpha \Big( \mathbb{E}_{s \sim \mathcal{D},\, a \sim \mu}\big[Q(s,a)\big] - \mathbb{E}_{(s,a) \sim \mathcal{D}}\big[Q(s,a)\big] \Big) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{TD}}(Q)$$

The first expectation is over the actions the policy would take, the second over the dataset. The result is a $Q$-function that is provably a **lower bound** on the true value under stated conditions, so a policy maximising it cannot be relying on an overestimate.

No behaviour policy needs to be estimated, and the regulariser drops into any actor-critic method — SAC, in the paper's implementation.

The pessimism is uniform, applied wherever the policy departs from the data, regardless of whether that departure is well-supported. When the dataset is narrow this is exactly right. When it is broad and high-quality, the penalty suppresses good actions that happen to be slightly off-distribution, and CQL underperforms methods that trust the data more.

The strength $\alpha$ controls this and there is no principled way to set it offline — the natural procedure would be to evaluate candidate values in the environment, which is the thing offline RL forbids. Offline policy evaluation is its own unsolved problem, and it means offline RL's hyperparameters are typically tuned by exactly the online access the setting rules out.

CQL is the strongest of the value-based answers to offline RL and became the standard baseline. What it does not question is the premise that offline RL should be dynamic programming with a correction.

Decision Transformer takes the other route: if the difficulty is that bootstrapping queries actions the data does not contain, do not bootstrap. Model the trajectory as a sequence conditioned on the return, train by supervised next-token prediction, and ask for a high return at test time. No $Q$-function, no max, no extrapolation to unseen actions — and, correspondingly, no ability to stitch together better behaviour than the data contains, which is what value-based methods can do and this cannot.

refs.t: Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning
Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning without Exploration
Offline Reinforcement Learning: Tutorial, Review, and Perspectives on Open Problems

dt.lead: Every method in this lane estimates values and bootstraps, and offline that is precisely what breaks. Decision Transformer discards the entire apparatus: treat a trajectory as a sequence of tokens, condition on the return you want, and train by supervised next-token prediction. There is no value function and no Bellman backup anywhere.

blocks.b:
A trajectory is tokenised as a repeating triple of desired return, state and action:

$$\tau = \big(\hat{R}_1,\, s_1,\, a_1,\; \hat{R}_2,\, s_2,\, a_2,\; \ldots\big), \qquad \hat{R}_t = \sum_{t'=t}^{T} r_{t'}$$

where $\hat{R}_t$ is the **return-to-go** — the reward actually accumulated from that point onwards in that trajectory. A causal transformer is trained to predict the action token at each position, by ordinary cross-entropy or regression. That is the whole training procedure.

At test time the desired return is specified as the first token, and the model produces actions consistent with achieving it; after each step the target is decremented by the reward received. Asking for a high return is a prompt, not an optimisation.

The model learns $p(a \mid \text{state}, \text{desired return}, \text{history})$ from data that contains trajectories of many qualities. Poor trajectories teach it what low-return behaviour looks like; good ones teach it high-return behaviour. Conditioning on a high return selects the latter.

This is upside-down: rather than finding the policy that maximises return, it models the relationship between stated return and behaviour, and reads off the branch it wants. Nothing is maximised, so nothing can exploit an overestimate — the failure that ruins offline value-based methods has no mechanism here.

The transformer's context also handles credit assignment differently. Attention connects a reward directly to an action many steps earlier, where a bootstrapped value must propagate it through every intermediate step, which is where TD methods accumulate error over long horizons.

The limitation is the mirror of the advantage. Dynamic programming can **stitch**: given trajectories that each solve part of a task, a value function can compose them into a better policy than any single trajectory demonstrates. Sequence modelling cannot — it reproduces conditional behaviour present in the data, and a return it has never seen is a prompt it cannot honour.

So on datasets requiring stitching, value-based offline methods clearly win, and the paper's own results show it. Conditioning on a return beyond the dataset's maximum also degrades rather than extrapolating, which is the expected behaviour of a conditional model and a disappointment to the natural hope.

Subsequent analysis found that a substantial part of Decision Transformer's reported advantage holds on datasets where stitching is not required, and that filtered behavioural cloning — train only on the best trajectories — is a surprisingly strong baseline in the same regime.

The lasting contribution is the framing. Casting control as sequence modelling means the whole transformer toolchain applies — scale, pretraining, multi-task conditioning, in-context adaptation — and Trajectory Transformer, Gato and the generalist agents that followed are built on it.

It also poses a question the lane had not asked: how much of reinforcement learning's machinery is essential and how much is a consequence of the era in which it was developed, when function approximators were weak and data was collected online. Decision Transformer's answer is partial — stitching is genuinely lost — but the question stands.

refs.t: Decision Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Sequence Modeling
Offline Reinforcement Learning as One Big Sequence Modeling Problem

apprentice.lead: Behavioural cloning copies what an expert did and can say nothing about why, so it cannot generalise beyond the demonstrated states. Apprenticeship learning tries to recover the **reward** the expert appears to be optimising, on the argument that the reward is the compact, transferable description of the task and the policy is not.

blocks.b:
Assume the reward is linear in known features, $R(s) = w^\top \phi(s)$. Then the value of a policy is $w^\top \mu(\pi)$, where

$$\mu(\pi) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t \phi(s_t) \;\Big|\; \pi\Big]$$

is its discounted **feature expectation**. If a learned policy's feature expectations match the expert's, then for **any** weight vector the two have the same value — so the learner is as good as the expert under the true reward without ever knowing what it is.

That turns an inference problem into a matching problem: find $\pi$ with $\|\mu(\pi) - \mu(\pi_E)\|$ small. The expert's side is estimated by averaging over demonstrations.

The method alternates. Given the policies found so far, find the weight vector that most separates the expert from all of them — a max-margin problem, solved as a quadratic program. Given that reward, solve the resulting MDP for its optimal policy and add it to the set. Repeat until no weight vector distinguishes the expert.

The output is a mixture over the policies found, whose feature expectations match the expert's; the paper is explicit that no single policy in the set need do so.

The cost is in the inner loop: every iteration solves a full reinforcement-learning problem to optimality. For anything beyond small discrete MDPs that is prohibitive, and it is the standing objection to the whole IRL family — GAIL's contribution is removing exactly this loop.

The reward that explains a set of demonstrations is not unique, and not nearly. A reward of zero everywhere makes every policy optimal, so it explains any demonstration; scaling a reward changes nothing; and adding a potential-based shaping term leaves the optimal policy identical.

Max-margin selects one by a criterion — separate the expert from the alternatives as widely as possible — that is a reasonable heuristic and not a principle. The resulting reward can be arbitrary in the directions the demonstrations do not constrain, and there is no statement about which of the many explanations is right.

That is the specific gap MaxEnt IRL closes, by choosing the distribution over behaviours with maximum entropy subject to matching the feature expectations — the least-committed choice, in a sense that can be stated precisely rather than argued for.

blocks.h: Why recover a reward at all
blocks.b:
The case for IRL over cloning is transfer. A reward function is a compact description of the task that remains valid when the dynamics change, the agent's body changes, or the initial states differ; a cloned policy is valid only where it was demonstrated.

That argument is why the line persisted despite its cost, and why it reappears in a different guise in language-model alignment: a reward model learned from human preferences is exactly an inferred reward, used to optimise a policy that no demonstration directly specifies. The ambiguity and the shaping-invariance problems come with it.

refs.t: Apprenticeship Learning via Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Algorithms for Inverse Reinforcement Learning

maxentirl.lead: Many reward functions explain the same demonstrations, and feature matching does not say which to choose. Maximum-entropy IRL resolves the ambiguity by a principle rather than a heuristic: among all distributions over behaviour consistent with the observed feature expectations, take the one that commits to nothing further.

blocks.b:
Instead of seeking a single optimal policy, model the expert as sampling trajectories with probability exponential in their reward:

$$P(\tau \mid \theta) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)} \exp\big(\theta^\top \mathbf{f}_\tau\big), \qquad Z(\theta) = \sum_{\tau} \exp\big(\theta^\top \mathbf{f}_\tau\big)$$

This is the maximum-entropy distribution subject to matching the expert's feature counts — the least-committed choice, in the precise sense that any other consistent distribution assumes something the data does not support.

It has a second virtue: it models **suboptimal** behaviour naturally. A human demonstrator is noisy, and a framework that insists the expert is optimal must attribute every deviation to a reward that rationalises it. Here better trajectories are exponentially more likely and worse ones merely less likely, so noise is expected rather than explained away.

The gradient of the log-likelihood has the standard exponential-family form:

$$\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L} = \tilde{\mathbf{f}} - \sum_{s_i} D_{s_i} \mathbf{f}_{s_i}$$

the difference between the expert's empirical feature counts and those expected under the current reward, where $D_{s_i}$ is the model's state-visitation frequency. Matching feature expectations reappears, now as the stationary condition of a likelihood rather than as the objective itself.

Computing $D$ requires a forward-backward pass over the MDP, analogous to the one used for hidden Markov models, and that is tractable only when the state space is small enough to sweep. The partition function $Z$ sums over all trajectories and is intractable in general — this is the same obstacle that dogs energy-based models throughout machine learning.

The paper's application is route prediction from taxi GPS traces, learning what drivers trade off between distance, time and road type. That grounding matters: it is a real dataset of genuinely suboptimal human behaviour, which is the case the framework is designed for and the case max-margin methods handle worst.

The formulation also connects the field to a large body of existing theory. A reward exponentiated into a distribution is an energy-based model, so everything known about them applies — including that the difficulty is always the normaliser.

blocks.h: The intractability, and how it was escaped
blocks.b:
Beyond small discrete spaces the partition function cannot be computed, so the method as stated does not scale. Guided cost learning uses sampling-based approximations to make it work in continuous domains with neural rewards.

GAIL then makes the sharper move. It shows that the occupancy-measure matching implied by this framework can be performed adversarially — a discriminator distinguishing expert from learner state-action pairs is implicitly the reward — which eliminates both the partition function and the inner reinforcement-learning loop that apprenticeship learning needed. The maximum-entropy framing survives in GAIL's entropy regulariser, so the principle outlived the algorithm.

refs.t: Maximum Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Guided Cost Learning: Deep Inverse Optimal Control via Policy Optimization

dagger.lead: Behavioural cloning is supervised learning on expert demonstrations, and it fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the classifier: the learner's own mistakes take it to states the expert never visited, where it has no training data, so errors compound. DAgger fixes the data distribution rather than the model.

blocks.b:
Supervised learning assumes the test distribution matches the training one. In sequential control it does not, because the policy **generates** the states it will be evaluated on. A small error moves the agent slightly off the expert's trajectory; the resulting state is slightly unfamiliar; the next error is larger; and the deviation grows.

The theory makes the cost precise. A classifier with error rate $\epsilon$ under the expert's distribution can incur regret growing as $T^2\epsilon$ over a horizon $T$ — quadratic, not linear, because each mistake changes the distribution of everything after it.

No amount of additional expert data fixes this, since more demonstrations only cover the expert's distribution better, and the problem is the states the expert never enters.

DAgger's loop collects data where the learner actually goes. At iteration $i$, execute a policy that mixes the expert and the current learner, $\pi_i = \beta_i \pi^\star + (1 - \beta_i)\hat{\pi}_{i}$, with $\beta_i$ decaying so control shifts to the learner. Record the states visited, and ask the **expert** what it would have done at each. Add those pairs to the dataset and retrain on everything collected so far.

The aggregation is the point — the classifier is refitted on the union, not just the newest batch, which is what makes the procedure a no-regret online learning algorithm. The guarantee that follows is linear rather than quadratic regret in $T$.

The labels are the expert's action at states the expert did not choose to be in, which is precisely the recovery behaviour cloning never observes: how to get back on track after a mistake.

The requirement is a queryable expert available throughout training, not merely a recorded dataset. For a human demonstrator that means labelling thousands of states out of context, one at a time, which is laborious and sometimes ill-defined — a person asked what they would do in a situation they would never have reached often cannot say.

Where the expert is an algorithm the requirement is cheap, and that is where DAgger is used most: distilling a planner or an expensive optimal controller into a fast reactive policy, or training a vision-based policy from a privileged expert with access to simulator state.

The mixing schedule for $\beta$ is another practical wrinkle, and the theory permits the simple choice of $\beta_1 = 1$ and zero thereafter.

DAgger and the IRL line answer the same complaint about cloning in opposite ways. IRL infers *why* the expert acted, on the argument that a reward transfers where a policy does not, and pays with an expensive inner optimisation and an ambiguous solution. DAgger keeps the cheap supervised objective and pays by demanding continued access to the expert.

Which is right depends on what is expensive. If expert queries are cheap and the task will not change, DAgger is far simpler. If demonstrations are fixed and the reward must transfer to new dynamics, the inverse route is the only option.

refs.t: A Reduction of Imitation Learning and Structured Prediction to No-Regret Online Learning
Efficient Reductions for Imitation Learning

gail.lead: Inverse reinforcement learning recovers a reward and then optimises it, with a full RL solve in the inner loop. GAIL removes the intermediate step: match the expert's distribution over state-action pairs directly, using a discriminator as the learned signal — which makes imitation an adversarial problem rather than a two-stage one.

blocks.b:
A policy induces a distribution over state-action pairs, its **occupancy measure** $\rho_\pi$. Two policies with the same occupancy measure are the same policy in every way that matters, so imitation can be stated as making $\rho_\pi$ match $\rho_{\pi_E}$ — a distribution-matching problem.

The paper's theoretical result is that running IRL and then RL is equivalent to matching occupancy measures under a particular regulariser, and that different regularisers give different imitation algorithms. Choosing the one corresponding to the GAN objective yields:

$$\min_{\pi} \max_{D} \; \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\log D(s,a)\big] + \mathbb{E}_{\pi_E}\big[\log(1 - D(s,a))\big] - \lambda H(\pi)$$

The discriminator is implicitly the reward. There is no separate reward-recovery stage, and no inner loop solving an MDP to optimality per iteration.

blocks.h: Why the policy cannot be trained like a GAN generator
blocks.b:
In an image GAN the generator is a differentiable map from noise to samples, so the discriminator's gradient flows straight back into it. Here the generator is a policy whose outputs pass through an environment, and no gradient crosses that.

So the discriminator's output is used as a **reward** — $-\log D(s,a)$, or a variant — and the policy is optimised by a standard policy-gradient method, TRPO in the paper. Reinforcement learning does the credit assignment over time; the adversarial game supplies the objective.

The entropy term $H(\pi)$ is the maximum-entropy framing carried over from Ziebart's IRL, so the connection to that line is explicit rather than incidental.

GAIL is far more efficient than behavioural cloning in **expert demonstrations** — a handful of trajectories suffices where cloning needs many — and it avoids the compounding-error failure, since the policy is evaluated on states it actually visits.

It is hungry in **environment interactions**, because every policy update needs fresh on-policy rollouts. The two costs are different resources, and which matters depends on whether demonstrations or simulation time is the scarce one.

It also inherits the adversarial family's instability wholesale: oscillation, a discriminator that becomes too strong and stops providing a useful reward, and mode collapse appearing as a policy that reproduces one expert behaviour and ignores the rest.

blocks.h: The reward it does not give you
blocks.b:
The discriminator is a reward in effect and not in a transferable form. It is trained to separate two specific distributions, so it is entangled with the dynamics it was trained under and does not survive a change of environment — which forfeits the main argument for doing inverse RL rather than cloning in the first place.

AIRL addresses that by constraining the discriminator's form so a disentangled reward can be recovered. And the discriminator-as-reward pattern reappears at scale in language-model alignment, where a preference model plays the same role — with the same caveat that what it has learned is entangled with the distribution it was fitted on.

refs.t: Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning
Learning Robust Rewards with Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning
Maximum Entropy Inverse Reinforcement Learning

planet.lead: World Models showed that a policy could be trained entirely inside a learned dynamics model, but it fitted its three parts one after another and evolved a controller of a few hundred parameters. PlaNet keeps the imagination and discards both the staging and the controller: one latent model trained alongside the data it gathers, and — in the paper's own words — no policy or value network at all. Every action is the result of searching the model afresh.

blocks.h: A state that both remembers and doubts
blocks.b:
The recurrent state-space model is the part of PlaNet that everything after it inherited, and its argument is that the two obvious designs each fail in a way the other does not.

A purely stochastic state — a classical state-space model — must carry every fact it will need through a sampled bottleneck at each step, and information leaks out of a sample. A purely deterministic state — a plain RNN — remembers perfectly and has exactly one future, so it cannot represent that it does not know what happens next, which is precisely the thing a planner needs to be told.

RSSM keeps both paths in one state. A deterministic recurrent component carries

$$h_t = f(h_{t-1},\, s_{t-1},\, a_{t-1})$$

and a stochastic component is drawn conditioned on it, $s_t \sim p(s_t \mid h_t)$, with a posterior $q(s_t \mid h_t, o_t)$ that additionally sees the observation. The prior must predict what the posterior infers; the gap between them, as a KL, is the entire pressure that makes the model able to imagine forward without looking.

The standard variational bound trains one-step predictions. The prior is asked to match the posterior one step ahead and nothing asks it to still be right ten steps ahead — but ten steps ahead is what planning consumes. A model can be excellent at the objective it was given and useless for the purpose it was built for.

Latent overshooting generalises the bound to every distance up to the planning horizon, adding KL terms between the posterior at time $t$ and priors unrolled $d$ steps from time $t-d$:

$$\sum_{d=1}^{D} \mathrm{KL}\big[\, q(s_t \mid o_{\leq t}) \;\|\; p(s_t \mid s_{t-d},\, a_{t-d:t-1}) \,\big]$$

Because the comparison is between latent distributions, the multi-step terms cost no image decoding — the expensive part of the objective stays at one step per frame while the consistency being trained is many.

This is the half of PlaNet that did not survive. Dreamer, built directly on the same state model a year later, reports flatly that it "did not find latent overshooting for learning the model … necessary". The RSSM was the durable contribution; the objective that motivated it was not.

There is no policy network. At each step the planner holds a Gaussian belief over action sequences of length $H$, samples $J$ candidates, scores each by summing the reward head's predictions along the imagined latent trajectory, refits the belief to the best $K$, and repeats $I$ times. It then executes the first action of the mean sequence and throws the rest away, replanning from the new observation — model-predictive control, with the cross-entropy method as the optimiser.

Evaluation never leaves latent space. Candidate sequences are scored by the reward head directly, so the decoder is needed for training and not for acting.

The data efficiency this bought is the headline result. Within 100 episodes PlaNet beats A3C trained from proprioceptive state for 100,000 episodes, on every task; after 500 episodes it matches D4PG trained from images for 100,000, with the finger task named as the exception; on cheetah run it exceeds D4PG's final score by 26%. Averaged over the suite the paper claims 200× less environment interaction — though the abstract itself says only "substantially fewer episodes", which the per-task spread justifies.

Planning at every step has three costs, and the next model in this line was built to remove them.

Deciding is a search rather than a forward pass, so action selection carries $I \times J$ model rollouts of length $H$ behind it. Nothing accumulates: each step's plan is discarded, and no amount of planning distils into anything reusable.

The binding limitation is the third. With no value network, a reward further away than $H$ steps does not exist to the planner — it cannot want something thirty steps out, and lengthening $H$ makes the compounding model error worse rather than better. Dreamer's ablation sweeps the horizon and shows exactly this shape: PlaNet's score depends sharply on it, while learning a value to estimate returns beyond the horizon makes Dreamer robust to it.

And the objective still reconstructs images, so capacity is spent on visual detail whether or not control needs it — the expense that MuZero's value-equivalent model avoids by never reconstructing anything at all.
